activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: A good pencil grip pinches the pencil between your thumb and first finger, resting it on your middle finger.
story:
Lily sat at Grandma's big table. She wanted to write her name all by herself. Grandma put a pencil in her hand. Lily grabbed it in her whole fist. She pushed the pencil onto the paper. The letters came out wobbly and fat. They did not look like L I L Y at all.

"Hmm," said Lily. "Why is my L so big and bumpy?" Grandma sat next to her. Grandma picked up her own pencil. She pinched it with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil rested on her middle finger. Grandma wrote her name, and every letter stood neat and small.

Lily looked hard at Grandma's hand. "Can I try that way?" Lily pinched the pencil with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil rested on her middle finger. She drew a line down. Then a little curve. It was an L! Lily made another L, and a tall stick, and a curl. "Lily!" she read out loud. Grandma clapped. On the empty page, Lily wrote her name three more times.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: Feeling nervous on the first day of school is okay.
story:
Henri woke up very awake. Today was his first day of school. He put on his red shirt. He ate his toast. Then his tummy felt funny. It felt like small wings were flapping inside.

"Mom, my tummy is fluttery," said Henri. Mom knelt down beside him. "My tummy felt that way on my first day too," she said. "It is okay to feel like that." Henri held her hand all the way to school.

At the classroom door, a boy was chasing a ball. The ball rolled right to Henri's feet. Henri picked it up and threw it back. The boy laughed. Henri's tummy stopped fluttering. Inside, the teacher held up a green triangle made of paper. Henri sat down on the small blue chair and smiled.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy.
story:
Josephine went to the park with Grandma. She wanted to find a red leaf. Grandma said, "Stay close to me." So Josephine stayed close. "Look, don't touch," Grandma said at the big fire pit. A man was making a fire to cook. Sparks flew up. The fire was hot. The bench in the shade was cold. Hot fire, cold bench. How did one feel so different? Josephine liked wondering about that.

Then they sat at a picnic table for a snack. Josephine saw something shiny on the ground. It was a little bottle. Inside were little red and yellow balls. They looked just like candy. Josephine wanted to pick them up. Her hand came close. Then she remembered her rule. Look, don't touch.

"Grandma!" she called. "I see candy on the ground." Grandma came right over. She looked in the bottle. "These are not candy," Grandma said. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine." Grandma picked up the bottle with a tissue and put it in her pocket. "Good girl," said a kind man with a dog. His dog began to beg for a piece of Josephine's apple.

Josephine gave the dog nothing. Grown-ups give the treats too. She sat by Grandma and ate her apple, all the way to the seeds.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: The alphabet starts with the letter A and ends with the letter Z.
story:
Brooklyn went to the bookshop with her dad. She saw books everywhere. Some were big. Some were small. "Can I look?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "I will sit right here."

Brooklyn found a book with letters in it. The first letter was A. "A," she said. "A says ah, ah, ah!" She turned the page. B came next. "B says buh," she said. She kept turning the pages. C, D, E, F. Each letter made its own sound. "How many letters are there?" she wondered.

She turned more pages. G, H, I. Then J, K, L, M, N, O, P. She stopped at P. "The letters stop here," she thought. "P is the last one." She closed the book. But then she heard a friendly voice singing. It was the bookshop lady. She was singing the letter song. Brooklyn listened.

The song went on and on. Q, R, S, T, U, V. Brooklyn opened the book again. W, X, Y. The song was not done yet! Then the lady sang, "Z!" Brooklyn looked at the last page. Z was there. The letter Z! The alphabet did not stop at P. It went all the way to Z. "Wow," said Brooklyn. "Z says zzz, like a bee!"

Brooklyn ran to Dad. "The alphabet starts at A," she said. "And it ends at Z!" Dad smiled. "Can we sing it?" asked Brooklyn. "After dinner," said Dad. "But we can look now." They looked at the letters together. Brooklyn pointed at Z and said, "Zzz!"

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot.
story:
Sara planted seeds at the farm. She put carrot seeds in one row. She put tomato seeds in another row. Then she watered them all. "Grow, little seeds," she said. "Grow, grow."

The next day, Sara forgot something. Which row had the tomatoes? She looked and looked. The soil all looked the same. "Oh no," she said. "I can't remember!"

Grandpa had an idea. They cut card into little signs. Sara drew a carrot on one. She drew a tomato on another. Grandpa pushed the signs into the soil. "Now the labels show what is in each spot," said Grandpa. Sara clapped her hands.

Every day Sara checked her garden. Tiny green leaves came up. She looked at the tomato label first. Then she found the baby tomatoes right there. "It worked!" she said. "It worked, it worked!"

Soon there were fat red tomatoes and long orange carrots. Sara washed one carrot with the hose. Her dog Buddy wagged his tail and dropped a bone at her feet, hoping for a share. Grandpa laughed. Sara bit her carrot and smiled. "Tomorrow we pick the tomatoes," she said.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: People say 'please' when they ask for something.
story:
Victor wanted apple juice at snack time. He saw the big jug on the table. He grabbed at it. "Give me juice!" he said. Miss Ana held the jug away. "Try again," she said. Victor felt his face go hot. He looked at his friend Sam. Sam said, "Juice, please." Miss Ana poured the juice right away. Sam got a full cup.

Victor took a big breath. He tried again. "Juice, please," he said. Miss Ana smiled. She poured. Victor got a full cup too. The juice was cold and sweet. He heard the little plink of Sam's cup on the table.

Then Victor bumped Sam's arm. Some juice spilled. "Sorry," said Victor. "It's okay," said Sam. "You can help me wipe it." They wiped the spill together with a paper towel.

After story time, Victor felt sleepy. His eyes blinked slow. "Miss Ana, can you help me find my coat, please?" he asked. Miss Ana handed him his red coat. "Thank you," said Victor. He put it on all by himself. "See you tomorrow," said Miss Ana.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A vegetable plant that does not get enough water droops.
story:
Harrison had three pots on the balcony. One pot, two pots, three pots. In the pots lived lettuce, a carrot, and a tomato plant. Dad stood by the door and watched.

One morning the sun was very hot. Harrison looked at his plants. The carrot stood tall. The tomato stood tall. But the lettuce was drooping. Its leaves hung down like sad little arms.

"The lettuce looks tired," said Harrison.

"Give it a drink," said Dad.

Harrison took his watering can. He poured the water on the soil. The smooth leaves got wet and shiny.

Harrison counted the drops. One drop, two drops, three drops, four.

Later he came back to look. The lettuce was standing up again. The leaves pointed up to the sun.

Harrison ran to Dad. "Come see!" he said. He pointed at the pot. "My lettuce woke up!"

Dad smiled. "It sure did," he said.

After lunch, Harrison got the mail with Dad. There was a letter for Harrison from Grandma. Inside was a sticker of a big red tomato.

Harrison held the sticker up to his pot. "Look, tomato," he said. "Someday you will be big too."

Then Dad gave Harrison a cookie. They sat in the shade and watched the little garden grow.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help.
story:
Joshua was in his bed. The room was dark. His blanket was soft and warm.

Then Joshua heard a sound. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window. Joshua felt scared. His tummy felt tight. He pulled the blanket up to his chin.

He remembered what Grandpa said one day. "You can tell me anything." So Joshua called out, "Mom! I hear a sound!"

Mom came fast. She turned on the little light. "Let's look together," she said. They stood by the window. Tap, tap, tap. Mom pushed the curtain aside.

A branch was tapping on the glass. The wind made it move. Joshua laughed. "It's just a tree!"

"Want to sleep with the curtain open a little?" Mom asked. "Then you can see it."

Joshua nodded. He felt happy now. Outside, the neighbor's dog began to bark. "Rufus is awake too," Joshua said.

Mom kissed his head. His pillow felt cool on his cheek. Joshua closed his eyes and listened to the soft tap, tap, tap.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth.
story:
Claare wanted to make soup for Grandma. She found a big pot in the toy box. She put in a pinecone, two leaves, and a small stone. "Stir, stir, stir," she said. The soup smelled like nothing at all. That was just fine.

Claare picked up the spoon. She held it to her mouth. She wanted a taste. Grandma sat close by in her soft chair. "Wait," said Grandma. "Pretend soup is for pretending." Claire looked at her pot. Then she made a big slurping sound. "Slurp! Mmm!" she said. Nothing went in her mouth. Grandma laughed and clapped. "That is the best soup I never ate," she said.

Claare fed her teddy bear next. "One bite, teddy," she said. She held the spoon to his fuzzy mouth. Teddy "ate" it all up. Outside, a bird began a song. Claire sang along. It was her last song before lunch. Then Grandma called, "Real soup is ready!" Claire ran to the table. Her bowl was warm, and Grandma held her hand.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: A flashlight helps you see into dark spots, like under a bed.
story:
Isaac climbed into the family car. He wanted his little blue dinosaur. It was his favorite toy. But where did it go?

"Did you lose Rex?" asked Mom. Isaac looked under his seat. It was too dark in there. He could not see a thing.

Mom reached into her bag. "Here, try this." She clicked on a flashlight. Isaac took it and pointed it down. The light made the dark spot bright. And there was Rex, lying under the seat!

"Rex!" Isaac grabbed him and hugged him tight. "He was hiding in the dark!" Mom laughed. "The light helped us find him."

Isaac held the flashlight up. He made the light go on the ceiling. He made it go on his shoes. "This is the best car day ever!" he said. Rex sat on his lap. Isaac clicked the light off, then on again. The seat went dark, then bright. "We will never lose you again, Rex," said Isaac. Mom started the car. "Home we go, with Rex and the flashlight too." Isaac waved the light at the window. "Bye bye, dark!" he said.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: You see colors with your eyes; you cannot tell a color by feeling it with your fingers.
story:
Natalie had a big yellow bag. The bag was full of toys. She could not see inside it. "Guess a toy!" said Dad.

Natalie put her hand in. Her fingers found something round. "A ball!" she said. She squeezed it. Yes, it was a ball. "It is a red ball!" she said.

She pulled it out. Oh! The ball was blue, not red. Natalie laughed. Her fingers told her it was a ball. But her fingers did not tell her the color. She had to look with her eyes.

She put the ball back in. Then she found something soft. It felt like a little bear. What color was it? She could not tell yet. Out it came. The bear was green! Natalie clapped her hands.

Then she felt something small and bumpy. Maybe a car? She pulled it out. Yes! A little red car. "I looked fast that time," she said. Dad laughed too. "One more?" he asked. Natalie's tummy felt hungry, but she said, "Just one more!" Her hand went in. Her nose came close to the bag. She felt a smooth, flat block. Out came a yellow block. Four toys on the rug, four colors to see. "My turn to fill the bag, Dad," she said.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: A tablet has a button you press to turn it on.
story:
Margot sat at the little table at school. A dark tablet lay in front of her. She wanted to draw a cat on it.

She tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened. She tapped it again and again. The screen stayed dark. "Why won't it wake up?" she asked.

Miss Ada came over. She did not say much. She took Margot's finger and put it on a small button at the side. She helped Margot press it down. The screen lit up. Margot's eyes got big. A press had made it work!

Margot pressed the button by herself next time. On came the screen. She found the drawing app and drew a big orange cat with a fat tail. It was winter outside, and the cat had a scarf.

When she finished, she did not leave the tablet on the table. She pressed the button again and turned it off. The screen went dark, just like before. She put the tablet back in the basket where it belonged.

"You did it all by yourself," said Miss Ada.

Margot smiled and drew a tiny sun in the air with her finger.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: In a pretend shop, one person can be the shopkeeper and another can be the shopper.
story:
Wesley was a small boy. He walked in the forest with his teddy bear. He wanted to play shop, but he had no one to sell to.

Wesley found a flat stump. He set it up like a little counter. He put three pinecones on it. "Shop is open," he said. He waited.

Then his big sister came down the path. "Hello," she said. "I am the shopper. You be the shopkeeper."

Wesley held out a pinecone. But his sister did not take it yet. She looked and looked. Wesley had to wait while she chose.

At last she pointed. "I want this one, please."

Wesley gave it to her. He carried the other pinecones home in his pockets, one for teddy and one for himself.

"Come back tomorrow," said Wesley.

"I will," said his sister, and she hugged him.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: A steady beat stays even and keeps going, like footsteps when you march.
story:
Gabriella sat on the small rug at Miss Jo's music studio. Miss Jo played "Mary Had a Little Lamb" on the piano. "Clap with me," said Miss Jo. Gabriella wanted to clap just right. But her claps went faster and faster. They ran away from the song. The song stopped and Gabriella frowned.

"Let's try something," said Miss Jo. She stood up. "March with me." Gabriella marched around the room. March, march, march. Her footsteps went even and kept going. She saw her feet stay steady. Then she clapped the same way her feet went. Clap, clap, clap. The claps stayed with the song now. "You did it!" said Miss Jo.

"Can I sing too?" asked Gabriella. She sang, "Mary had a little sheep." Well, she sang "lamb," but close. Miss Jo played and Gabriella clapped and sang all together. Miss Jo gave her a big smile and a sticker shaped like a star.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'sorry' shows you feel bad when you hurt someone or make a mistake.
story:
Hazel went to the library with Mama. She wanted a book about a chicken. The shelves were big. She could not see the top.

Hazel walked fast. Her elbow hit a boy's tower of blocks. Crash! The blocks fell down. The boy made a sad face. Hazel said, "Sorry." He said, "That's okay." They put the blocks up again. The tower stood tall. The boy smiled.

Then Hazel asked the librarian, "Please, where is the chicken book?" The librarian pointed. There it was! "Thank you," said Hazel. The book was fresh from the shelf. It smelled like paper. On the way home, her bag swung by her side. Mama read the book at bedtime. The chicken said, "Cluck, cluck!"

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card.
story:
Logan held his grandma's hand at the library door. He wanted a card of his own. His friend Mia had one. She could take books home.

Logan walked to the big desk. He stood on his toes, but he was too small. "I want a card," he said. The librarian smiled. "A grown-up helps a child sign up," she said. Grandma sat down on a soft chair. She patted her knee. Logan climbed onto her lap. Grandma wrote on the paper. Logan wrote his own name, slow and wobbly. His L came out a little loose at the bottom. "Good try," said Grandma.

Then the librarian handed Logan a small blue card. It had his name on it. He picked out a book about trucks. He held the card out. Beep! The book was his to take home. "I will thank the trucks," Logan said. Grandma laughed. Logan put the card in his pocket, nice and safe.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Words are all around us, on signs, labels and boxes, and they tell us things.
story:
Emily was at Grandpa's house. She wanted a cookie. She could smell them baking.

Grandpa's kitchen had lots of boxes. Each box had little marks on it. Emily pointed at the marks. "What is that?" she asked. Grandpa smiled. "Those are words," he said. "Words tell us things."

Grandpa held up a box. "This box says OATS," he said. He held up another. "This one says SUGAR." Emily looked and looked. The words were everywhere. They were on the big jar. They were on the little tin.

Grandpa's cat came in. The cat rubbed her soft neck on Emily's leg. The dog pushed his slimy nose into Emily's hand. Emily giggled. Then she pointed at a big book on the table. "Does that have words too?" she asked.

"It does," said Grandpa. "We read the front page first. Then we turn each page." Grandpa opened the book. He read to Emily while the cookies cooled.

Emily leaned on his arm. "Read the words again," she said.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street.
story:
Dylan woke up in his bed. He could hear Mum in the kitchen. He ran to find her. "Can we go to the park today?" he asked.

"Soon," said Mum. "First, porridge." Mum put the pot on the stove. Dylan saw steam rise up. "The pot is hot," said Mum. Dylan did not touch. He sat at the table. He ate his crunchy toast instead.

After breakfast, Dylan put on his shoes. Then he looked out the window. He could see the park across the road. He could see the swings. He wanted to run straight there. But the road had cars. The cars went fast. Dylan stopped at the front step. He waited. "Mum, hand please," he said.

Mum smiled and took his hand. They looked left. They looked right. No cars came. They walked across together. At the park, Dylan held the gate for a little girl. "Thank you," she said. Dylan ran to the swings. Mum sat on the bench and waved. "Watch me go high!" Dylan called. "I'm watching!" said Mum.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Saying "Let's pretend" tells your friends a game is starting.
story:
Stella stood by the blocks at school. Two kids were rocking baby dolls. One stirred a pretend pot on the toy table. Stella wanted to play too. But she did not know how to start.

She walked closer. She stood and watched. The kids did not look up. Stella asked herself a question. What would make them see her game? Then she had an idea.

"Let's pretend I am the dog," she said. She got down on her hands. She gave a little scratch behind her ear. The girl with the doll laughed. "Dogs need a basket!" she said. She tipped a basket over and put a small blanket in it. The boy patted the basket. "Here, dog, here," he called.

Stella crawled in and curled up. The baby doll was tucked in beside her. "Lucky dog," said the girl. "You get to stay home with the baby."

Stella wagged her pretend tail and barked once, very softly.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: String instruments like guitars and violins need tuning so their notes sound right.
story:
Zoey stood in the garage with her dad. A little guitar sat on a wood bench. It was hers, and she wanted to play a song.

She plucked the strings. The sound was funny. It went boing and blurp. Zoey made a mean face at the strings. "You sound silly," she said. She plucked again. Boing, blurp.

Dad knelt down next to her. "Let me try something," he said. He turned the little pegs on the guitar. Zoey watched. He turned one peg a tiny bit. Then he plucked a string. The note sounded clear and sweet.

"Again!" said Zoey. She plucked the string herself. It sang out nicely now. She plucked the next string. That one still went blurp. Dad turned its peg too.

Zoey tapped her foot and played. Boing went one string. She pointed at it. Dad turned that peg. Then Zoey played all the strings, one by one. Each note came out right.

She played her first song in the garage. Dad clapped. Zoey hugged the guitar against her chest. "Play it again," said Dad. So she did.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: A backpack is a bag you carry on your back.
story: Sienna stood at the school playground gate. Her new backpack sat on her back. It was very full. She had packed her bear, three cars, and a big book. The backpack was so heavy that she fell over on the soft grass. "Oh no," said Sienna. A boy named Tom ran to her. "Your bag is too full," he said. Sienna sat up and opened it. She took out the cars. She took out the big book. Now the bag was thin and light. She felt the cool air on her back. Sienna stood up and marched to the slide. Her bear rode on her back. "I did it!" she called. "Slide with me!" said Tom. Down they went, whoosh, into the sand.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: Ten is written with two digits, a 1 and then a 0.
story:
Adam made a tower at school. It had ten blocks. He wanted to write ten on paper. Miss Kim gave him a fresh sheet and a fat crayon. Adam sang the counting song to himself. One, two, three, all the way to ten. Then he wrote the numbers. He wrote 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Then he stopped. Ten needed more room. Adam asked, "Where do I put ten?" Miss Kim said, "Right after nine." Adam looked at her paper. Ten was not one number. It was a 1 and then a 0, side by side. Adam copied it. "One and zero," he said. "That makes ten." He taped the paper on his tower.

Outside, Maya dropped her leaf. The wind pushed it away. Adam picked it up and gave it back. Maya smiled. Adam took a big bite of his apple at snack time. Then he counted his crackers. "One, two, three," he said. Maya had none left. Adam gave her one. "Now you have one," he said. Maya laughed and held up her cracker. "Ten blocks, one cracker," she said. Adam pointed at his paper in his pocket. "Ten is one and zero," he said. "That one goes first."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: When both teams have the same score, it is called a tie.
story:
Georgia sat on Grandpa's big soft chair. Grandma sat beside her. Uncle Ben sat on the floor. Everyone was watching the game on TV.

Georgia was wearing her striped pajamas. The players ran fast. Everyone yelled, "Go, go, go!" Georgia clapped her hands. "Go, go, go!" she said too.

Then the whistle blew. The game stopped. Uncle Ben said, "Two for the red team. Two for the blue team." Georgia pointed at the TV. "Who won?" she asked. Grandpa said, "The same score. The same. It is a tie." Georgia frowned. "Nobody won?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "Nobody won. A tie."

Georgia waited. The players came back out. They ran some more. Georgia clapped again. "Go, go, go!"

The whistle blew one more time. Grandpa held up his hands. "Four for red. Four for blue. A tie again!" Georgia stood up on the chair. "A tie again!" she said. Uncle Ben laughed. Grandma gave her a kiss on her head. Outside, the night was dark and quiet. Georgia waved at the TV. "Bye bye, tie," she said. "Bye bye, game."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: An ice cube feels cold when you touch it.
story:
Rehmat ran to the backyard. Her water cup sat on the little table. The sun was hot on her head. She saw the shiny table shining in the light. Then she heard her grandma call, "Rehmat, come get some ice!"

Rehmat looked in the bowl. The ice cubes looked like tiny mountains. She picked one up with her fingers. "Ooh!" It felt so cold. She dropped it fast. Plip! It fell into her cup. She touched the cup. The cup was cold now too. She put her nose near it. She smelled nothing at all. Then she took a tiny sip. The cold water tasted good on the hot day.

A bee buzzed by her ear. Rehmat heard its buzz. She stood very still and watched it fly away. Grandma came out with a hat. "Here, so the sun stays off your face." Rehmat touched the soft hat and smiled. "Thank you, Grandma," she said, and drank her cold water.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Small toys can roll or slide under furniture like couches and beds.
story:
Colton went to the grocery store with Mama. He held his little red car in his hand. "Stay with me," said Mama. Colton walked by the cart.

Then Colton saw the big apples. He let go of the car to touch one apple. The apple was cold and round. "Apples," he said.

When Colton looked down, his car was gone. "Oh no," he said. "My car!" He looked by the apples. No car. He looked by the cart. No car.

A kind worker came over. Her name tag had a big smile on it. "Can I help you look?" she asked. "Yes," said Colton. "My red car rolled away." They looked under the shelf. It was low like a couch at home. And there it was! The car had rolled under the shelf, just like toys rolled under his bed at home. The worker had thick gloves on. She reached way down and pulled the car out.

"Thank you," said Colton. He gave her a big smile. Later, at home, Colton took his crayons to draw the nice worker. He drew her smile too. "There," he said. "That is my helper."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: At the playground, go down the slide feet first.
story:
Leo ran to the big slide at the park. Mama held his hand on the way. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Leo stayed close.

At the slide, a girl named Mia climbed to the top. She lay down with her head pointing down. Leo watched. Mia's tummy rubbed on the slide. "Ouch," she said. The slide felt rough that way. She sat up and turned around. Then she went down with her feet first. She landed soft in the sand. "That was fun!" she said.

Leo climbed the steps. He wanted to go down, too. He started to lie down with his head first. Then he stopped. He sat up tall. He turned around. He went down with his feet first. Whee! He landed soft in the sand. Leo kicked his feet and laughed.

Mama waved from the bench. Leo ran back to her. "Stay close," said Mama. Leo held her hand. Then they went to the slide again, feet first.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Holding up one finger for each thing you count helps you keep track of the number.
story:
Peyton sat at the big table in math club. "Today we count shells," said Ms. Rosa. She put down two piles. "Which pile has more?"

Peyton looked and looked. She wanted to say the right one. She counted the first pile. "One, two, three, four." Then she forgot. "Oh no," she said. "I lost my number!"

Her friend Leo giggled. "Numbers are sneaky," he said. Peyton laughed too. Then she had an idea. She held up her hands. She touched one finger for each shell. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven fingers stood up tall. They stayed up. They would not sneak away.

She counted the second pile. "One, two, three, four, five." Five fingers. "Seven is more than five!" she said. Ms. Rosa smiled and gave Peyton a sweet cookie. Peyton picked the big piece. "Seven fingers," she said, wiggling them all, "are very hungry fingers."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Measuring cups and spoons help cooks put in the right amount of each thing.
story:
Amira was at school. Today the class would bake cookies for her family. The cookies would be little sheep. Amira wanted them to be nice.

First came the sugar. Amira picked up the bag. She tipped it over the bowl. Sugar poured out fast. Too much sugar! A big white hill sat in the bowl.

Her teacher came over. She did not look mad. She showed Amira a small cup. Amira spooned sugar into the cup. She filled it up. Then she tipped it into the bowl. Just the right amount!

Amira looked at the cup. Now she knew what it could do. She used it for the flour too. Then the little spoons for the butter.

Her teacher put the sheep cookies in the oven. Amira watched from her chair.

Soon the cookies came out. They were warm and bumpy like sheep. Amira carried them home in a box.

"Cookies!" said her baby brother. He reached out one small hand. Amira gave him the biggest sheep of all.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A new baby will often hold tight to a finger placed in its hand.
story:
Brielle sat in the nursery room. Sun came in the little window. The baby was in the crib. He was her new baby brother. He was so cute.

Brielle wanted the baby to look at her. She clapped her hands. The baby did not look. She made a soft face. "Hello, baby," she said. The baby still did not look.

Then Mommy said, "Try your finger, Brielle." Brielle put one finger near the baby's little hand. The baby's fingers closed around it. He held on tight! Brielle giggled. "He has my finger!" she said. She counted his little fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." The baby held on and on. Brielle smiled and waited. Mommy sat in the sun by the crib. "My finger, my finger," said Brielle softly. The baby held tight, and the room was quiet and warm.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: A grown-up should check that bath water is warm, not hot, before you get in.
story:
Bennett ran into the backyard. The sun made the water table warm. "Splash time!" he said.

He wanted to fill a big bucket. The hose sat by the tall fence. Bennett knew to stay close to Grandma. He ran back to her chair. "Can I turn on the water?" he asked.

Grandma came with him. She turned the tap. Bennett put his hand under the water. "Ow! Hot!" he said. He pulled his hand back fast.

"The sun made the hose hot," said Grandma. She let the water run. She put her own hand in it first. "Now it is warm," she said.

Bennett touched the water. It felt nice, not hot. He filled the bucket all the way. Then he splashed his little boat. "The water is just right," he said.

Grandma sat in her chair by the light of the evening. Bennett stayed near her. "Do it again tomorrow?" he asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "We will always check the water together."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: If you paint on one half of a paper and fold it while the paint is wet, the paint prints onto the other half.
story:
Sebastian sat at the big table in the library. Miss Jo put out paper and paint. The paint felt smooth and cool on his fingers.

Sebastian wanted to make a butterfly. He painted one wing on one half of his paper. He painted it red. "One wing," he said. "Only one."

Then his elbow bumped the paper. It folded in half on the wet paint. "Oh no," said Sebastian.

He opened the paper slowly. There was the red wing. And there was another wing beside it! Two wings, the same size. "Miss Jo, look!" he said.

"That is a fine butterfly," said Miss Jo.

Sebastian painted a yellow wing on a new paper. He counted, "One wing, two dots." Then he folded the paper. He pressed it with his flat hand. He opened it again. Two yellow wings, and four dots.

"I want more colors," said Sebastian. He dug into the paint cups for blue. He painted a blue wing on one half of the paper. Fold, press, open. Blue wings, matching like twins.

At home in the kitchen that evening, Sebastian hung his butterflies on the fridge. "Red one, yellow one, blue one," he said. His mother clapped.

Sebastian smiled at the blue wings. "Fold it again," he whispered to the paper.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups.
story:
Jules sat at the dinner table. He was scared of the big pot. It went hiss, hiss on the stove. Dad lifted the pot with two big mitts. "Dad, does the pot scare you too?" Jules asked. "Yes," said Dad. "So I use the mitts. Then I am not scared."

Jules felt happy. He banged his spoon. "Yay, noodles!" he said. Then his fork went clatter on the floor. His lip went down, down. He felt sad. Mom picked up the fork. She gave him a clean one near his plate. His sad face went away.

Dad took one bite. Steam came up. "Ow, hot!" said Dad. His face turned red. He looked angry at the noodles. "Dad, you have feelings too?" asked Jules. Dad laughed. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups." Jules clapped. "Even me!" he said. Then he took a tiny bite. The noodles went slurp. "Excited for more!" said Jules. Dad smiled and filled his bowl again.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A week has seven days.
story:
Noah stood at the train station. He held his papa's hand tight. The big train puffed in. The doors opened. Out stepped Grandpa with a red bag.

"Grandpa!" Noah ran to him. Grandpa picked him up high.

"I will stay for one whole week," said Grandpa.

At home, Mom hung up the paper calendar. Noah got his crayon. He drew one big dot on Monday. "Grandpa came today," he said.

Each day, Noah drew one dot. Tuesday. Wednesday. Thursday. Friday. Saturday. Grandpa helped him make pancakes. Mom stirred the bowl. Noah watched the eggs sink into the flour.

On Sunday, Noah counted his dots. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." He jumped up and down. "Seven days! That is a week!"

"You counted it right," said Grandpa.

The next morning, they went back to the train station. Grandpa waved from the window. The train puffed away.

Noah looked at his dots. "Come back soon, Grandpa," he said.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: Writing your name on your things helps them find their way back to you.
story:
Sadie stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her new lunchbox with two hands.

At lunch time, Sadie sat down. A boy sat next to her. He had a lunchbox just like hers. It was red with a boat on it. So was hers.

"Hey, that is mine," said the boy. "No, that is mine," said Sadie. They both looked sad. Then the teacher came over. She opened one lid. "S-A-D-I-E," she read out loud. "This one says Sadie."

Sadie smiled big. The other lunchbox had the boy's name inside. He was called Tom. Sadie gave Tom his lunchbox. Tom gave Sadie hers. After lunch, they went to the art table. They used a big brush to stir the paint. Tom painted a boat. Sadie painted her name.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange.
story:
Levi stood at the paint table. He wanted to paint a big pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. The pots said red, yellow, blue. "Red, yellow, blue," Levi said. He counted them. "One, two, three." No orange at all.

Levi looked at his pumpkin. He looked at the pots. He dipped his brush in red. Then he dipped it in yellow. He stirred them on his paper. The red and yellow swirled like a thin ribbon. Then, like magic, they turned orange! Levi opened his mouth. "Orange!" he said. His pumpkin could be orange now.

Levi painted the pumpkin round and bright. It looked like a giant orange egg sitting in a green field. He painted a thin stem on top. The teacher came to see. "What a big pumpkin," she said. Levi smiled. "I made the orange myself," he said. He held up his brush. On it was one drop of red and one drop of yellow.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Sharing means letting someone else use something too.
story:
Everett ran to the swings at the playground. The sky was cloudy, but the swings still shined like magic ships. He wanted the red swing most of all. But a girl was already on it.

"My turn soon," said Everett.

"Okay," said the girl. "One, two, three, then you."

She counted, and she hopped off. Everett got on. He flew so high he almost touched a cloud.

Then Everett saw a boy by the tree. The boy had no shovel for the sand. Everett had three shovels in his bucket. All three.

Everett looked at the shovels. He looked at the boy. The boy was digging with just his hand.

"You can use this one," said Everett. He held out the red shovel.

"Thank you," said the boy.

Now they dug together. They made a giant sand cake under the tree. "Let's pretend to cook it," said the boy. They patted the sand and counted, "One, two, three!"

The girl came over too. "I want to cook," she said. Everett gave her the blue shovel. She added leaves on top.

"Best cake ever," said Everett.

"Best cake ever," said the boy.

"Best cake ever," said the girl, and she put one more leaf on top.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot, so only grown-ups touch it.
story:
Wyatt wanted warm milk for his teddy bear. He carried teddy out to the backyard. The grass was wet with morning dew. Teddy got a little wet too.

"I will make you warm milk," Wyatt said. Inside, Dad stood by the stove. The pot sat on top. The stove did not look hot. There were no flames at all. Wyatt stepped near and reached out his hand.

"Stop," Dad said. "Let me check." Dad held his hand high above the pot. "Still hot," he said. "Only I touch the stove." Wyatt stayed close to Dad. He watched and waited.

Soon the milk was warm. Dad poured a little cup. Wyatt took a small taste. It was warm and sweet. He gave teddy a sip from his own cup. "Only grown-ups touch the stove," Wyatt said to teddy. Then they sat down on the dry step together.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: In the song 'Five Little Monkeys Jumping on the Bed', one monkey falls off each time, so the number gets one smaller.
story:
Margot sat at the dinner table. She had five toy monkeys with her. She wanted to sing her monkey song before she ate.

"Five little monkeys jumping on the bed," she sang. "One fell off and bumped his head!" She put one monkey under her chair. How many were left now? She counted them. One, two, three, four.

Papa put her warm bowl of soup down. "Sing it again," he said.

"Four little monkeys jumping on the bed. One fell off and bumped his head!" Margot put another monkey under her chair. She counted again. One, two, three. Each time she sang, one more monkey went away.

"Two monkeys left," said Margot. "Then one. Then zero monkeys!" She peeked under her chair. All five monkeys sat together. They were not scary at all. They looked like a little owl family sitting in a tree, all in a row.

"Time to eat," said Papa. Margot picked up her spoon. "Pretend the soup is monkey stew," she said. Papa laughed. "Eat it slow," he said, "one spoon, two spoons, three."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cooks rinse dirt off vegetables like carrots and potatoes before cooking them.
story:
Matthew went to the farmers' market with Dad. There were big tents and lots of apples. A farmer had a basket of carrots. The carrots were orange and long. They still had dirt on them.

"We can make carrot soup," said Dad. Matthew held the carrots all the way home. He saw dirt on his hands. "Yuck," said Matthew. "The carrots are dirty."

At home, Dad filled the sink with water. Matthew put the carrots in. He rubbed them with his fingers. The water turned brown. Matthew scrubbed and scrubbed. Soon the carrots were shiny and clean.

"Look, Dad!" said Matthew. "The dirt came off!" Dad smiled. Mom came in to help cook. She used the big knife to cut the carrots. Matthew watched from his chair.

Mom put the pot on the stove. Matthew could not touch the hot stove. He sat on his stool and waited. Soon the soup was ready. Matthew wore his bib like a big cook. "I made this soup!" he said. Everyone ate the warm soup. "The dirt came off, and now we eat clean carrots," said Matthew. Dad gave him a hug and a shiny spoon.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Pockets in a coat can hold small things like mittens.
story:
James was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. James wanted to play in the snow.

"Put on your coat," said Grandma. James tried to put it on by himself. He pushed his arms in. He got one sleeve stuck. Grandma helped him find the other arm. Then James pulled the zipper up, little by little. It went all the way to the top!

James ran outside. He made snowballs. Soon one mitten fell off in the snow. James looked and looked. He found it under the sled.

Then James saw his coat pocket. He opened it. It was big enough for two mittens. James put both mittens inside. He zipped the pocket shut.

"I did it!" said James. "My mittens have a home now."

"You are thirsty from all that play," said Grandma. "Come in for warm milk and a sandwich."

"Thank you, Grandma," said James. He patted his pocket. The mittens stayed safe and warm inside.
